newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen official says Maskhadov to win outright.
newsitem.headline: Chechen official says Maskhadov to win outright.

text.p: Aslan Maskhadov, who led Chechnya's tiny guerrilla army to victory over Russian forces last year, is likely to be elected president outright after a first round of voting, a electoral official said on Tuesday.

"There's a very great likelihood he'll go through on the first round," Bilal Ozdemirov of the Central Electoral Commission told reporters as counting continued after Monday's presidential and parliamentary elections across the mountainous Moslem region.
He said with ten to 20 percent of votes counted, hardline guerrilla leader Shamil Basayev was in second place. Maskhadov needed 50 percent to avoid a second-round run-off.
Ozdemirov said turnout at 9 p.m. (1800 GMT) on Monday, an hour before polls closed, was estimated at 61 percent or 265,000 votes. Polling was extended by two hours to cope with long queues.
The Central Election Commission has declared the poll valid, saying well over the required 50 percent of eligible voters had cast their ballots.
Speaking outside the Commission headquarters in devastated central Grozny, Commission member Ozdemirov said Maskhadov led in virtually every polling station across the region which had returned data.
Maskhadov's margin over Basayev was generally greater than that between Basayev and the third-placed candidate, acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, Ozdemirov said.
A preliminary result could be available "towards lunchtime", he added.

The elections are a crucial step in restoring order and stability in the region still heavily scarred by 21 months of fierce fighting between Russian troops and rebel guerrillas bent on proclaiming Chechnya a fully independent state.

Over 100 foreign observers are in Chechnya to monitor an election for the first time. Several observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said they were impressed by the smoothness of the process.

Maskhadov, a 45-year-old former Soviet artillery colonel, is popular with voters not just for leading their tiny guerrilla army to victory last August but for the quiet level-headedness he showed in peace negotiations with Moscow in the autumn.
"I see our land flourishing under Maskhadov. He has more experience (than the others)," said one elderly man dressed in a a handmade sheepskin coat, after casting his vote.

Basayev is likely to do much better in the southern mountain districts around his home base of Vedeno. But the trend among voters questioned on Monday in the main centres of population and among war refugees bussed over the border from neighbouring regions was clearly in favour of Maskhadov.

A victory for Maskhadov would be greeted with some relief in the Kremlin. A win for Basayev, who is wanted as a "terrorist" in Russia, would be a nightmarish embarrassment for President Boris Yeltsin, who has admitted sending troops to crush Chechen independence in 1994 was a big mistakes.

All the candidates, however, are committed to turning the de facto independence secured by the withdrawal of Russian troops last year into full-fledged sovereign statehood -- something Moscow refuses to countenance.

Maskhadov has pledged to restore order to a region awash with weapons and to work with all the guerrilla leaders to avert Chechnya sinking into Afghan-style anarchy. He also wants Moscow to make good on promises of aid to rebuild the shattered economy, which was based on oil refining and pipelines.
